ARTICLE IN PRESS The relationship between tourism, economic growth and environmental sustainability: empirical evidence from major tourist destinations Abstract The positive impact of tourism on the economy of countries and their increasing commitment to this practice has led to numerous studies in the literature, from the emergence of the TLGH at the beginning of the century to the present day. However, destinations are no strangers to the negative externalities generated by tourism. These negative externalities respond to a harmful impact on the environment, which, together with the increasing concern of governments for the environment, has also aroused the interest of the research field. Therefore, this study, using a technique that is not widely used, focuses on the analysis of tourism, economic growth and the environment in those countries that have been part of the top 10 tourism countries during the period 1995-2023. The analysis reveals a variety of causality results. Finally, policy recommendations for improvement are made on the basis of these results. INTRODUCTION The importance of the tourism sector has been widely reflected in the literature over the past two decades through numerous articles. Specifically, the relationship between tourism and economic growth has been examined in a wide range of countries, using various indicators to analyse both tourism-related and economic variables (Alcalá-Ordóñez et al., 2024; Brida et al., 2016). These studies to date have consistently demonstrated the positive contribution of the tourism sector to the economies of tourism-receiving countries. In this regard, it is essential to consider the impact of tourist flows on the creation of both direct and indirect employment, due to the sector’s multiplier effect, which influences other sectors (Gao et al., 2021), as well as on local production (Badimo and Yuhuan, 2024). Due to these positive effects generated by tourism activity, the relationship between tourism and the economic growth of destination countries has attracted significant interest since the S formulation of the Tourism-Led Growth Hypothesis (TLGH) by Balaguer and Cantavella-Jordá S (2002). E R Nevertheless, in addition to the positive effects reported in empirical literature, tourism also entails P a series of negative externalities, for example, through increased pollution due to greenhouse gas emissions. Given the growing concern in recNent years over environmental preservation and sustainability, incorporating the environmeIntal dimension into the tourism–economic growth nexus is now essential, taking into accoEunt the numerous articles published during the last years (Jambor and Leitao, 2017; Kumail eLt al., 2022; Mester et al., 2023; Mishra et al., 2019; Waheed C et al., 2020; Zhang and Gao, 2016; Zhang and Zhang, 2021). The development of activities such I as sustainable tourism has helped mitigate some of the negative impacts associated with tourism T (Ben Jebli et al., 2019R). However, other detrimental effects must also be considered, such as urban overcrowdingA and increased waste generation in visited locations (Puig-Cabrera and Foronda-Robles, 2018). Therefore, considering the well-established influence of tourism on economic growth and incorporating the environmental dimension, in response to the increasingly global concern for environmental protection, the objective of the present study is to analyse the empirical relationship between tourism, economic growth, and the environment in countries that have ranked among the world’s top ten tourist destinations from 1995 to 2023. The rising global concerns regarding climate change and resource depletion, sustainability has become a central pillar in the analysis of tourism impacts. The 2030 Agenda for sustainable development, underscores the need to integrate environmental considerations into tourism planning and policy. Recent conceptual development establishes the difference between weak and strong sustainability. The former assumes substitutability between natural and human capital, while the latter emphasizes the irreplaceable nature of environmental assets. Regenerative tourism, with a current rising importance, goes beyond sustainability by aiming to restore and improve environmental and social conditions at destinations (Go & Kang, 2023). METHODOLOGY This study analyses the relationship between tourism, economic growth, and the environment at the level of a group of leading countries in the reception of international tourists over the last three decades, in line with the United Nations' Sustainable Development Agenda (Go and Kang, 2023). The seminal analysis of the Tourism-Led Growth Hypothesis (TLGH) conducted by Balaguer & Cantavella-Jordá (2002) has been complemented by the incorporation of environmental factors, specifically by including the effects that tourism activity has on the environment. Thus, the objective is to reduce the impacts generated by tourism, making it sustainable, while simultaneously measuring its relationship with economic growth (Kyara et al., 2022). Therefore, the study aims at the pursuit of sustainable growth that goes beyond pure economic growth, encompassing development concepts such as environmental sustainability (Li et al., 2018). S 4.1. Cross-sectional Dependence S E The case study analysed in this work, although it is a panel of data from different countries from R a macroeconomic tourism perspective, conducts an aPnalysis between the three regions in which these countries are integrated (Europe, America, a nd Asia). The unit of analysis is each of these N countries, but within their respective region or geographical area. Given this level of analysis, it is I expected that the evolution of tourism, economic growth, and environmental quality is not E independent among the different defined geographical areas. Due to various national public L policies or the interconnection between the countries (e.g., through transport or trade), C dependence between the anaIlysed countries may arise. Westerlund Cointegration Test Considering that the series exhibit non-stationary processes, the existence of long-term relationships between tourism, economic growth, and environmental pollution at the level of the different countries within each of the geographical areas studied becomes plausible. CONCLUSIONS This paper provides an innovative analysis of the relationship between tourism, economic growth, and pollutant emissions. A key contribution of this study lies in its regional approach, which reveals differentiated patterns across the analysed territories. On the one hand, it incorporates the potential externalities generated by tourism into the analysis of the TLGH, and on the other S hand, it adopts a geographical regional approach, as opposed to most studies in the scientific S literature, which focus solely on country-level analysis. This study analyses 15 countries that have E ranked among the top 10 global tourist destinations in terms of foreign tourist arrivals during the R period 1995-2023, using the number of arrivals as the tourism variable, and employing a full panel P of countries. To enhance the robustness of the a nalysis, the countries are divided by region: N Europe, America, and Asia. The study applies a test to detect potential cross-dependence among I the analysed countries using the CS-ARDL method, allowing for both short- and long-term E estimates while considering this dependency, and complementing the work with a causality L analysis. C The results confirm a signIificant relationship between tourism, economic growth, and T environmental impact across the 15 countries studied from 1995 to 2023. The CS-ARDL model R has allowed for distinguishing short- and long-term effects, showing that tourism drives economic A growth, while GDP and CO₂ emissions are strongly correlated, reflecting the traditional relationship between development and pollution. However, the environmental impact of tourism varies by region. In the short term, tourism has a positive effect on GDP, but its relationship with CO₂ emissions differs: in Europe, it is associated with a more sustainable model; in America, it drives economic growth without a clear effect on pollution, and in Asia, its impact is not significant on either variable. In the long term, GDP remains the main driver of CO₂ emissions, and while tourism boosts economic growth in Europe and America, this effect is not relevant in Asia. Additionally, in America and Europe, high levels of pollution can negatively affect GDP, whereas in Asia, the relationship between development and emissions is stronger and bidirectional. Finally, the Granger causality test confirms the interdependence between tourism, economic growth, and CO₂ emissions, with bidirectional relationships in the group of countries. However, regional differences are evident: in Europe and Asia, tourism drives GDP, while in America, this relationship is inconclusive. In all regions, economic growth contributes to increased emissions, ARTICLE IN PRESS but only in Asia is there a possible feedback effect of pollution on the economy. It should be noted that the countries included in this study are all leading global tourism destinations. This practice prioritizes environmental care, which can be achieved through awareness programs and providing tourists with information, without sacrificing the benefits that tourists gain from each trip. Likewise, reducing transportation use is necessary. In recent years, the increase in electric vehicles, both private and public, whether large or small-scale (such as bicycles, motorcycles, etc.), has been significant, but cities should invest even more in these alternatives as a means of reducing pollutant emissions. This also facilitates local benefits, such as P employment, among other factors. Specifically, recommendations include promoting low-carbon tourism models in Europe, balancing tourismN development with emissions mitigation in the Americas and decoupling economic growthI for environmental degradation in Asia. JSON: Name: tourism_gdp_co2_cs_ardl Title: Estimating short- and long-run causal links between international tourist arrivals, real GDP, and CO2 emissions in major tourist destinations using a cross-sectional ARDL (CS-ARDL) framework Short Hypothesis: Controlling for cross-sectional dependence and GDP, year-to-year increases in international tourist arrivals Granger-cause increases in national CO2 emissions in the short run for countries that ranked among the top ten tourist destinations during 1995–2023. Related Work: Existing empirical work on the tourism–growth–environment nexus has used a mix of approaches: single-country ARDL/VECM studies that recover short- and long-run dynamics but ignore cross-country spillovers; panel cointegration estimators (FMOLS, DOLS) that estimate long-run coefficients but often assume slope homogeneity and omit short-run dynamics; panel VAR/PVAR frameworks that capture intertemporal interactions but require strong stationarity and large T; and common-correlated effects (CCEMG/PMG) methods that allow for unobserved common factors but differ in how they separate short- and long-run effects. Standard panel unit-root and cointegration tests have been applied variably, often without accounting for cross-sectional dependence or heterogeneous slopes. Limitations across prior approaches include inadequate control for cross-sectional dependence and global shocks, limited separation of short- vs long-run causal channels, heterogeneous slope bias when pooling, inconsistent lag-selection procedures, sparse regional disaggregation, and narrow tourism measures (arrivals vs spending or intensity). Few studies combine robust cross-sectional dependence testing, panel unit-root/cointegration procedures, CS-ARDL estimation, and systematic regional robustness checks on the same dataset. Abstract: This research pipeline specifies an empirical protocol to quantify short- and long-run causal relationships among international tourist arrivals, real GDP, and CO2 emissions for countries that featured among the world’s top ten tourist destinations between 1995 and 2023. The approach centralizes a CS-ARDL estimator that explicitly models cross-sectional dependence via common correlated effects while delivering both error-correction long-run multipliers and short-run dynamics. The pipeline prescribes pre-estimation diagnostics (Pesaran CD, CIPS unit-root, Westerlund cointegration), lag selection via information criteria, and inference with heteroskedasticity-robust and bootstraped standard errors. Key contributions are (1) an explicit testable workflow for separating short- and long-run tourism–environment linkages under cross-country spillovers, (2) region-level replication (Europe, Americas, Asia) and ablation studies (alternate tourism/environment measures; inclusion/exclusion of pandemic years), and (3) a standardized set of baselines and diagnostics for comparative evaluation. Expected outcomes are robust estimates of directional effects and regional heterogeneity that inform policy interventions for decoupling tourism growth from emissions. Experiments: Datasets: annual panel 1995–2023 for 15 countries (France, Spain, Italy, UK, Germany, Greece, Austria, Turkey, Poland, USA, Mexico, Canada, Thailand, Japan, Malaysia). Variables: international tourist arrivals (WTO), real GDP (constant 2015 USD, World Bank), CO2 emissions (Gg CO2 equiv., EDGAR). Preprocessing: winsorize variables at 1st/99th percentiles, compute per-capita variants, check VIF. Diagnostics: Pesaran CD test for cross-sectional dependence, CIPS panel unit-root test, Westerlund panel cointegration (bootstrap). Primary estimator: CS-ARDL with cross-sectional averages; lag selection by AIC/BIC; inference via cluster-robust SE and 1,000-block bootstrap. Baselines: pooled ARDL (no cross-dependence correction), panel FMOLS, panel DOLS, CCEMG (Common Correlated Effects Mean Group), panel VAR (PVAR). Causality test: Dumitrescu-Hurlin panel Granger causality. Evaluation metrics: statistical significance and sign of short-run coefficients and long-run multipliers; Error Correction Term significance and speed; out-of-sample 1- and 3-year forecast RMSE and MAE for model predictive comparison; Diebold–Mariano tests between CS-ARDL and baselines; robustness judged by coefficient stability across winsorization, per-capita measures, exclusion of 2020–2021, and regional subsamples. Ablation studies: (A) CS-ARDL without cross-sectional averages; (B) replace tourist arrivals with tourism receipts and with arrivals per km2; (C) include energy consumption and trade openness as additional controls; (D) estimate separate models for Europe, Americas, Asia. Report: coefficient tables (short-run, long-run), ECT t-stats, Granger causality matrices, forecast error comparisons, and sensitivity plots across ablations. Risk Factors and Limitations: Modeling risks: incomplete control of endogeneity if omitted time-varying confounders (energy mix, transport modal shifts, policy changes) correlate with tourism and CO2; mis-specification of lag lengths may bias short-run dynamics; cross-sectional averages may not capture heterogeneous common factors fully. Data risks: measurement error in international arrivals (reporting differences), CO2 allocation and emission inventory revisions, and missing or inconsistent tourism expenditure data; pandemic years (2020–2021) create structural breaks that challenge stationarity and cointegration. Statistical limitations: small cross-section (N=15) limits the power of heterogeneous estimators and subgroup inference; finite-sample bias in bootstrap inference for panel estimators; potential nonlinearities or threshold effects (EKC/Kuznets-type dynamics) are not modeled by linear CS-ARDL. Generalization limits: sample restricted to historically top tourist destinations reduces external validity for lower-tier or developing destinations. Computational constraints: extensive bootstrap and robustness grids increase compute time and memory, particularly for regional and ablation analyses.
